summary: All 16 units were read in full and every numeric key, worked example and table value was recomputed independently in Python, including a full classical-lamination calculation (Q-bar, A, effective moduli for [0], [0/90]s, [+45/-45]s and quasi-isotropic CFRP, plus the glass/epoxy cases), Arrhenius ageing times, Hollomon-Jaffe, Koistinen-Marburger, Weibull, WLF, Maxwell/Kelvin-Voigt, Faraday corrosion rates, anode-life and Ashby-index calculations. No wrong numeric key, tolerance, unit or answer-key letter was found, and directions of effect (Voigt/Reuss bounds, galvanic anode/cathode, Hall-Petch, Orowan, TTT/CCT shifts, tempering and ageing trends, index exponents and selection-line slopes) are all correct; TTT/CCT and ageing data are labelled illustrative/typical and are physically sensible (nose at 550 C, Ms about 220 C, no bainite on continuous cooling). The only substantive problem is one MCQ option that states a false fact (PEEK glass transition above 200 C) and contradicts its own explanation; the rest are minor wording, consistency and small-omission issues. String scans found no tabs, control characters, format placeholders, e+06 numbers, non-Latin garbling, stale option-letter references or '[object Object]'. This is an AI review: the course still needs a subject-matter expert before engineering reliance.

issues.problem: The keyed option d says PEEK's "glass transition and continuous-use temperature are well above 200 C". PEEK's Tg is about 143 C (as stated in the lesson table and in the question's own explanation), so the option is false and contradicts the explanation; a student learns that Tg of PEEK exceeds 200 C.
issues.suggestedFix: Reword option d to something like "PEEK, because its continuous-use temperature (about 250 C) is above 200 C, its melting point is about 343 C, and its chemical resistance is excellent", and in the explanation note that 200 C is above Tg (143 C) but PEEK, being semi-crystalline, retains useful stiffness there.

issues.problem: Hook: "Along the leg the material is stiffer than steel at a quarter of the weight". With the unit's own carbon/epoxy data E_L is about 139 GPa, below steel's 210 GPa; only the stiffness per unit mass is higher.
issues.suggestedFix: Say "as stiff as steel at about a fifth to a quarter of the weight" or "stiffer than steel per kilogram" (E/rho is about 90 against 27 GPa per Mg/m3).

issues.problem: Slip-system table lists HCP (Zn, Mg, Ti) with the basal plane (0001) as the main slip plane. This is right for Zn and Mg but not for titanium, whose dominant room-temperature slip is prismatic <a> slip. The '3 systems' count also gives only 2 independent basal systems.
issues.suggestedFix: Say "Zn, Mg (basal); Ti slips mainly on prism planes", and note that the 3 basal systems are only 2 independent.

issues.problem: The Burgers vector b is used in the Orowan and Taylor equations (b = 0.286 nm for Al, 0.256 nm for Cu) but is never defined or related to the lattice (b = a/sqrt2 for FCC <110> slip) anywhere in the module, although dislocation mechanics is the module theme. The Orowan expression Gb/L is also a simplified form (often 2Gb/L or Gb/(L-d)) and is not flagged as approximate.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a sentence defining the Burgers vector as the lattice displacement of the dislocation (|b| = a/sqrt2 for FCC, giving 0.286 nm for Al with a = 0.405 nm), and mark Gb/L as an order-of-magnitude form.

issues.problem: Classification table lists "rails" as a medium-carbon (0.25 to 0.60 %) use and "rail heads" as a high-carbon (0.60 to 1.4 %) use; rail steels are about 0.6 to 0.8 % C.
issues.suggestedFix: Remove rails from the medium-carbon row and keep rails and rail heads under high carbon.

issues.problem: Table says 6061-T6 is "easily formed and welded". 6061 is readily welded, but the T6 temper is not readily formed (forming is done in O or T4) and welding softens the heat-affected zone, losing much of the T6 strength.
issues.suggestedFix: Say "good corrosion resistance, weldable (with HAZ softening), formed in the annealed or T4 condition".

issues.problem: This unit uses E = 110 GPa for titanium (E/rho = 24.8), while the selection module uses E = 114 GPa for Ti-6Al-4V (beam index 2.41). Both are plausible but the course states two values for the same alloy.
issues.suggestedFix: Use one typical modulus (for example 114 GPa, giving E/rho = 25.7) in both modules.

issues.problem: Property table gives toughened zirconia K_Ic as "7 to 10" MPa m^1/2, whereas the next unit's table, q003 explanation and q010 marking guide give "6 to 10".
issues.suggestedFix: Use the same range (6 to 10) in both units.

issues.problem: Text before the equal-survival relation says the stresses are related "by the first expression in the equation below", but the equation block contains only one expression.

The marking guide of q009 expects mention of the standard linear solid (and the unit is expected to cover which model describes which phenomenon), but the lesson never introduces the standard linear solid or its relaxation and retardation time constants; it gives only Maxwell and Kelvin-Voigt.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a short paragraph on the three-element (standard linear solid) model, with its instantaneous modulus, relaxed modulus and relaxation time, or remove the reference from the marking guide.
